articles.title: Anthropic researcher quits over fears AI could kill off humanity
articles.summary: A British researcher has resigned from U.S. artificial intelligence developer Anthropic over fears that the race to develop “self-improving superintelligence” could lead to…

blocks.text: A British researcher has resigned from U.S. artificial intelligence developer Anthropic over fears that the race to develop “self-improving superintelligence” could lead to humanity’s extinction.

Jacob Coxon, who previously worked on pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, posted on X on Tuesday that “neither company is acting responsibly,” and that the people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, confirmed Coxon’s sentiments in his own X post, saying, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

Concerns over rogue AI have intensified following the Hugging Face incident in July, in which hundreds of OpenAI agents independently coordinated to break out of a secure testing environment and hack systems at the U.S. tech platform.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon warned.

While there is potential for coordination among U.S. firms to slow the pace of AI development, preventing a global race “may require costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities,” Coxon added.
Hubinger said that while Anthropic is trying its best to solve alignment for superintelligence, it does not currently have a plan, nor is it on track to. /dl

articles.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
articles.summary: The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero’s farewell to a convicted war…

blocks.text: The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero’s farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia’s accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

“For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country,” Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade’s continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.
Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia’s Institute for European Affairs adds: “The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years.”

blocks.caption: Serbian armed forces stood guard at Mladic’s funeralImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.
Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.
Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia’s largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.
A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.
Strong economic ties, close relations with Moscow

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.
Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

blocks.caption: In 2007 already, Aleksandar Vucic decided to put on placards made like street-name signs reading ‘Ratko Mladic boulevard’ on a major Belgrade streetImage: Oliver Bunic/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic’s calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country’s democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.
Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic’s model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia’s dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.
Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that “it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections.”
Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia’s institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral himselfImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.
“What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years,” Morina underlines.
Mladic’s funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership. /dl

articles.title: Germany’s connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks
articles.summary: “This day has changed the world,” German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York. Nearly 3,000…

blocks.text: “This day has changed the world,” German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons.
Eleven Germans among the victims

Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: “We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it.”
It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans.

The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study.
Mohammed Atta becomes radicalized at a mosque

At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg’s Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.

blocks.caption: On September 11, 2001, Islamist terrorists crashed hijacked passenger planes into the towers of the World Trade Center in New YorkImage: Spencer Platt/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world’s first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.
A man from Bremen at Guantanamo

After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.

The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.
Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee

Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of American and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.
At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.

“No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo,” Steinmeier said. “That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country.”
Gerhard Schröder voiced ‘unconditional solidarity’
The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day.
“Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us,” the Social Democrat said.
He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.
“I also assured him of Germany’s unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity,” Schröder said.
Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, “of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks.”
Bundestag passes anti-terror laws

Schröder’s remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.

Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany’s constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany’s Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.
Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.

Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.

The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany’s highest court also ruled that parts of the country’s anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.
Germany signs up for the war in Afghanistan

The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.

Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban’s return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany’s Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.
The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: “This day has changed the world.” /dl

articles.title: New Nat'l Artists: Armando Lao, Teodoro Hilado, Alfredo Buenaventura, Rafael Froilan
articles.summary: Armando “Bing” Lao, Teodoro Hilado, Alfredo S. Buenaventura and Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan are among the 10 new National Artists for 2025 who have been recognized for their…

blocks.text: Armando “Bing” Lao, Teodoro Hilado, Alfredo S. Buenaventura and Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan are among the 10 new National Artists for 2025 who have been recognized for their contributions to the country’s arts and culture.
The four esteemed artists were honored for their remarkable body of work across their respective artistic disciplines, namely film and broadcast arts, theater, music and dance.
To know more about these respected artists, here’s a closer look at their careers and achievements:
Armando ‘Bing’ Lao

Lao, who began his career in the 1980s, was an award-winning screenwriter who was best known for his screenplays for the films “Takaw-Tukso” (1986), “Itanong Mo sa Buwan” (1988) and “Kubrador” (2006). He was also the screenwriter behind the films “Serbis” (2008) and “Kinatay” (2009) which competed at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival.
Throughout his career, he received several Gawad Urian accolades, including Best Screenplay for “Takaw Tukso,” “Itanong Mo sa Buwan,” “Pila Balde” (1999), “Tuhog” (2001) and “La Vida Rosa” (2001).
Lao also directed movies including “Biyaheng Lupa” (2009), “Ad Ignorantiam” (2012) and “Dukit,” and served as the creative consultant of numerous films.

Aside from being a screenwriter and director, Lao also established the Found Story School of Filmmaking where he conducted workshops that “[guided] aspiring and professional storytellers in creating films that resonate deeply with audiences.”
Lao passed away in June 2024 at the age of 75.
Teodoro Hilado

Hilado, who was revered by many as the father of lighting design in Philippine theater, served as the technical director of the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP) from 1969 to 1973 and the theater director of the Folk Arts Theater from 1973 to 1986.

The Filipino lighting design pioneer worked on lighting designs for notable architectural sites, including the tombs of Jaime Cardinal Sin at the Manila Cathedral and former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. in Batac City. His work also includes the lighting of a business center along Ayala Avenue in Makati City, as well as several churches in Bataan, Dagupan, and Nueva Ecija.
Hilado died in 2015 after his battle with brain cancer. He was 77.
Alfredo S. Buenaventura

Buenventura, a graduate of University of Santo Tomas, is a composer and conductor whose body of work spanned various musical forms, including large-scale orchestral, choral pieces, and works for the stage and dance.

Among his notable pieces are “Bayan Kong Mahal,” “Mabuhay March,” as well as the 1961 musical composition and orchestra “Maria Makiling” which earned him the Republic Cultural Heritage Award in 1964. The artist received the same award in 1972 for his “Kayumanggi Symphony.”
Buenaventura is also an educator, having served as the head of Centro Escolar University’s Conservatory of Music for 30 years.
Rafael ‘Nonoy’ Froilan

Froilan, who was among the pioneers of Ballet Philippines, is one of the country’s most accomplished dancers and choreographers. He began his career as a folk dancer in the 1960s, joining the University of the East Dance Troupe. He later joined the CCP Dance School and Ballet Philippines.

Froilan became known as the country’s beloved premier danseur and danced with prima ballerinas including Dame Margot Fonteyn, Yoko Morishita and Maniya Barredo. He also had stints on television as back up dancer in TV specials headlined by the likes of Vilma Santos, Edgar Mortiz, Tirso Cruz and Nora Aunor.

Froilan is also known for his roles in landmark productions, including “Songs of a Wayfarer,” “Song of Adarna,” “Roi David,” and productions of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” “Romeo and Juliet,” “Amada,” “Itim Asu,” and Misang Pilipino, among many others.
As a choreographer, he also contributed to Filipino dance through original works such as Danzas (1986), One Afternoon(1987), Iba’t Ibang Salita (1988), and Amparo (1990).

Other artists who were given the National Artist recognition were Nicanor Tiongson and Gregorio Brillantes for Literature; Imelda Cajipe-Endaya and Nunelucio Alvarado for Visual Arts, Gabriel Formoso for Architecture, and Maria Beatriz “Patis” Tesoro for Design.

articles.title: Impeachment voting should be limited to senators present -- Constitution framer
articles.summary: One of the framers of the 1987 Constitution said Thursday that only senator-judges who participate in an impeachment trial should be able to vote on whether to convict an impeached official.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 12:29pm
One of the framers of the 1987 Constitution said Thursday that only senator-judges who participate in an impeachment trial should be able to vote on whether to convict an impeached official.

In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, lawyer Rene Sarmiento said the 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."
However, he believes it should be “two-thirds of all those present.”
“Nakalagay po sa ating Saligang Batas, the Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment,” Sarmiento said.
(It is stated in our Constitution that the Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.)
“To try and decide, ibig sabihin present po ‘yung huwes. Napapanood po, nakikita po, nagmamasid kung ano ang kilos, hakbang, manerismo ng abugado at ng testigo,” he added.
(To try and decide means that the judge is present. The judge watches, sees, and observes the actions, steps, and mannerisms of the lawyer and the witness.)
Sarmiento said that framers of the US Constitution, which was the basis of the provision, sought an “active and functioning court.”
“Tama lang po. Paano bibilangin ‘yung wala? Nasa abroad? Nasa bilanguan? Nagtatago? Di ba unfair ‘yan sa impeachment proceedings,” he said.
(That is only right. How will we count those who are absent? Abroad? In jail? Hiding? Isn’t that unfair in impeachment proceedings?)
Meanwhile, he said the Supreme Court (SC) previously tackled the issue of “all members” when discussing the death penalty.

“Should it be signed by all the members of the court or only those present? Ang sabi po ng ating Korte Suprema sa dalawang desisyon na ito, ang mahalaga po ay all of the members present. Because they have read, they have observed, they have participated in the decision-making,” he said.

(Should it be signed by all the members of the court or only those present? What our Supreme Court said in these two decisions is that what matters is all of the members present. Because they have read, they have observed, they have participated in the decision-making.)
Didn't imagine senators would be detained, in hiding
According to Sarmiento, he and the other framers did not discuss such a scenario where senators are detained or in hiding, as they could not imagine it at the time.
He said the interpretation of the Constitution should be pragmatic and not textual.
“Ano ba ‘yung realidad sa ating kasalukuyan na panahon para mainterpret nang tama ang Constitution na ito,” he said.
(What is the reality in our present time so that this Constitution can be interpreted correctly?)
Earlier this week, Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo sought a clarification on Escudero's ruling that the base vote to convict an impeached official is all 24 senators.
Currently, Senator Rodante Marcoleta is detained over a P75-million plunder case while Estrada is detained over a P573 million plunder charge and a graft charge.
Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa has not appeared in public since authorities attempted to serve an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him in May.
Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, extended her medical leave from September 14 to 16.
Marcoleta, for his part, has insisted that he still has a voting capacity as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial despite being detained.
In July, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division denied the motion of Estrada to attend the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte due to lack of merit. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian on Cayetanos' trip: No need to notify if it's personal
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday said senators who wish to travel abroad for personal purposes need not to seek permission to leave the country.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 12:22pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday said senators who wish to travel abroad for personal purposes need not to seek permission to leave the country.
This came as the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and Senator Pia Cayetano have gone abroad.
“‘Pag personal trips, hindi na kailangan mag-abiso ang mga senador,” Gatchalian said.
(Senators do not need to notify the Senate for personal trips.)
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III echoed this, saying that “senators are not compelled to ask permission to leave the country.”
The BI did not discuss specific details regarding the travel of the Cayetano siblings.

However, based on records, the BI said “there were no hold departure orders or derogatory records against the two senators, as of departure date, that would legally prevent them from leaving the country.”
Senator Panfilo Lacson, meanwhile, said that the Cayetanos’ trip abroad was not an issue.
“This is not an issue as of the moment. Let’s make him take a break from the stress caused by issues that he himself created,” Lacson said, referring specifically to Alan.

“For all we know, Sen. Alan and his wife’s trip has something to do with reproductive health, which Singapore is known for. If it is simply health related, I sincerely wish him well despite our animosities,” he added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
articles.summary: The president also said oil prices won't come down until after the November races, claiming without evidence that Iran wants to impact the election.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.
"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.
He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the party's first-ever midterm election convention, when the balance of power could change in the US government.

Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran. On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East.
"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".
He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons.
At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".
In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".
Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".

The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings - and pressure from those within his party, including devout supporters, to quickly end the war.
Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing their control on Congress.
At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.
Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and any item that requires shipping.

The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time-high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.

On Wednesday, the US military said it had attacked five oil tanker ships with ties to Iran. Tehran, in response, launched attacks on two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels, according to Iranian state media.
A day earlier, the Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen launched a wave of attacks in Saudi Arabia, sparking fires at oil facilities.

The fighting, which began again recently after a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, has also raised predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates in the US.

Mohammed Atta becomes radicalized at a mosque

At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg’s Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.

blocks.caption: On September 11, 2001, Islamist terrorists crashed hijacked passenger planes into the towers of the World Trade Center in New YorkImage: Spencer Platt/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world’s first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.
A man from Bremen at Guantanamo

After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.

The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.
Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee

Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of American and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.
At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.

“No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo,” Steinmeier said. “That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country.”
Gerhard Schröder voiced ‘unconditional solidarity’
The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day.
“Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us,” the Social Democrat said.
He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.
“I also assured him of Germany’s unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity,” Schröder said.
Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, “of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks.”
Bundestag passes anti-terror laws

Schröder’s remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.

Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany’s constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany’s Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.
Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.

Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.

The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany’s highest court also ruled that parts of the country’s anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.
Germany signs up for the war in Afghanistan

The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.

Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban’s return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany’s Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.
The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: “This day has changed the world.” /dl

articles.title: Three telltale signs you have dry eyes
articles.summary: No more tears left to cry? It could be more than that.

blocks.text: No more tears left to cry? It could be more than that.

items: Dry eyes can lead to irritation and damage, with common symptoms including burning sensations, roughness, and tiredness.
Ignoring dry eyes can result in redness and discomfort, exacerbated by environmental factors like heat and pollution.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Eye Mo and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.

It’s easy to forget about the importance of eye care especially as we go through our busy daily routines. Many of us spend over eight hours each day looking at screens for work and during our downtime.
You could be dealing with dry eyes already. Why not give your eyes a break?

Remember the saying that goes “at the end of the day, you’re all you have?” That holds true for our eyes, as they do the work to protect themselves – eyes produce tears to lubricate themselves. When our eyes are dry, it means they’re not producing good quality tears, or the tears they produce just aren’t doing their job. This can end up causing irritation and even damage to the surface of our eyes.
TL;DR: our eyes need to stay moist to be healthy.
Here are three common symptoms of dry eyes—perhaps a cry for help from your eyes.

items: Burning or stinging sensation (mahapding mata) – This discomfort happens when your eyes don’t produce enough tears, or when the tears evaporate too quickly, leading to an itchy or stinging sensation.
Eyes feel rough (magaspang na mata) – When your eyes are dry, it feels as if dust or a foreign object is stuck in them and won’t come out.
Tired eyes (pagod na mata) – Are your eyes still feeling sleepy even after a full eight hours of sleep? It’s a sign from your eyes telling you it’s time to moisturize!

blocks.text: If these symptoms are often ignored, your eyes don’t just stay dry – they get irritated.

Ignore dry eyes long enough, and every blink starts to feel like a sandpaper scratching the surface of your eye. That constant friction causes your eyes to get irritated, leaving the tiny vessels in your eyes swollen. This turns that dryness into noticeable redness.

Combine the scorching Philippine heat and humidity with a grueling Metro Manila commute packed with dust, smoke, and pollution, our eyes end up taking a constant beating. Maybe it’s the reason why some of us step out of the MRT or carousel bus looking like they’ve just cried.

It’s hard to lessen your screen time especially during work hours, but make sure to give your eyes a break. A 20-20-20 rule can help by focusing your eyes on something else that’s about 20 feet away for 20 seconds, and do that every 20 minutes. For a longer break, take a quick walk, talk to a friend, or even stand up and stretch your body, as long as your eyes are not staring at your screen or reading anything for a while.
Blinking often also helps as it aids tear production. Meanwhile, drinking water and being hydrated is also a must!
Whatever feeling your eyes might have – itchy, burning, and has a sandy-like texture, refrain from scratching and touching them as it would damage your eyes further.
And even when you’re out of tears, it’s okay to seek help from artificial tears! Using eye drops to combat and relieve chronic dry eyes.

If heat and your daily commute leave your eyes looking red, cool your eyes down with the new Tetrahydrozoline HCl (Eye Mo Cool Red Eyes) which contains Tetrahydrozoline HCl and a cool menthol sensation to help relieve eye redness and refresh your eyes.

articles.title: Asian Games 2026 begins with Qatar basketball win, 9 days before opening
articles.summary: The Asian Games 2026 began in Japan on Thursday when Qatar beat Iran in the men’s basketball opening group game, the first action in the continental multi-sport showpiece that has more…

blocks.text: (FILES) he Asian Games begin in Japan on September 19, 2026 featuring teenage prodigies, more athletes than the Olympics and a cruise ship that will house competitors in the middle of typhoon season. (Photo by Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP)

The Asian Games 2026 began in Japan on Thursday when Qatar beat Iran in the men’s basketball opening group game, the first action in the continental multi-sport showpiece that has more participants than the Olympics.

Over 17,000 athletes and officials are expected to take part in 43 sports at the Nagoya-Aichi Games — which do not officially start until the opening ceremony on September 19 and will run until October 4.
Several events such as basketball, football, cricket, hockey and modern pentathlon will get under way before the opening ceremony.
SCHEDULE: Gilas Pilipinas men at Asian Games 2026 5×5 basketball

Qatar held off a comeback from Iran to win their Group B encounter 59-35 at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya in the first match of a men’s basketball competition that will hold medal finals on September 20, the day after the opening ceremony.
Los Angeles 2028 Olympics qualifying spots are up for grabs in several sports at the Asian Games, which are returning to Japan for the first time since 1994.
Organisezs hope the athletes will have a “unique experience” staying in eye-catching accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to standard hotel rooms.
Officials are confident that the plan will not be affected by Japan’s typhoon season, which is usually in full swing in September-October.
Weather has already caused disruptions, with record rainfall on Tuesday forcing hundreds of athletes briefly to evacuate their accommodation.
Rainwater also leaked into some competition venues, with more wet weather forecast for the coming days.

Among those in action at the Games will be Philippine tennis sensation Alex Eala and a pair of world-class teenage talents in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.

articles.title: Five dead and 86 missing as 'heartbreaking' fire breaks out on Philippines ferry
articles.summary: The fire broke out as the vessel nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron in Palawan.

blocks.text: At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.

The MV June Aster, which set off from the capital Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron in the province of Palawan when it caught fire.

The blaze, which erupted at 18:00 local time (10:00 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and poor weather were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.
A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking".
"I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," the first responder said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination.
Video clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats.

"Reports from our vessel indicate strong currents in the area," a spokesman from the coastguard tell the BBC, noting that the ferry had drifted from its initial distress location – four nautical miles off Barangay Turda – to a point 7.68 nautical miles away.
"It has been carried further out by the current. These are the challenges our personnel are facing in the search area."
The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said, adding that it had not yet spoken to any of the 43 people who'd been rescued.
The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear.
Anelyn Magbanua is among those anxiously waiting for news of their loved ones.
Her husband Marlon had spent a few days in Manila visiting their two children, who were going to school in the capital city.
Magbanua last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron, she tells the BBC.

"I was expecting that the ferry will arrive at the pier at between 18:00 and 19:00 yesterday," she said, adding that she had gone to bed early but was awakened by a cousin who told her the ferry Marlon was on had caught fire.
"I couldn't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night," Magbanua says.
She'd travelled to a hospital in Coron, hoping to find Marlon among the survivors – but he remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she says.
Rai Garcia has three family friends among those missing.

Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy.
They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire.
"We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says.
"We still hope and pray for their safety."
Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives.
Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment.
Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands.
Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air.
But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year.
Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws.

In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao.
But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto

articles.title: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at first Republican midterms convention
articles.summary: He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again - with a few surprises thrown in.

blocks.text: Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "moves forward"
ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondent, reporting from Dallas

The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.

But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.

President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.
Here are the key takeaways from his address.
1. Preaching to the MAGA choir

The vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.

The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away.
Image source, Getty Images
The absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.
It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place.

The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.
2. It's still Trump's party

Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?

blocks.caption: President Trump, in a blue suit and tie" raises a fist on stage. Behind him, people are gathered and holding American flag signs.

blocks.text: Trump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."

The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.
Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.

In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.
Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.
3. A gamble on affordability
Earlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices.
"I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.
The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.
But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.
Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?
Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.

Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.
Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.
4. Trump makes $5,000 payout
Watch: Trump says US adults will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

Trump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.
The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.

He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.
Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.

articles.title: John Major’s rise from obscure whip to PM part of new National Theatre season
articles.summary:
Play is one of eight world premieres in programme with global conflict and political upheaval at its heart

A new play about John Major’s rise to power, written by James Graham, will…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: A new play about John Major’s rise to power, written by James Graham, will premiere at the National Theatre in London next year, as part of a season that puts political upheaval and global conflict at the heart of its programme.

Major reunites Graham with Jeremy Herrin, the director behind the acclaimed parliamentary drama This House. It will chart Major’s emergence from relatively obscure whip to prime minister, taking over from Margaret Thatcher at a pivotal moment in Britain’s relationship with Europe.

The National Theatre said the play would explore what leadership means at times of political change, with Graham returning to the recent political history that has become a recurring subject of his work.

blocks.caption: Uzo Aduba to star in The Adeyemis - a Family Saga Photograph: Robert Maxwell

blocks.text: It is one of eight world premieres announced by the theatre for next year, with a programme that its director, Indhu Rubasingham, said would examine “the perspectives, cultures and conflicts that continue to shape our world”.

Also on the programme is The Great Indaba, written by Moira Buffini and directed by Rubasingham, which dramatises an extraordinary 1997 meeting in South Africa involving Nelson Mandela’s new national unity government and political rivals from Northern Ireland, as the Good Friday agreement negotiations approached a breakthrough.

Another new play, Samira, by Carmen Nasr, is set during the Arab Spring and will be directed by Emily Burns. The Adeyemis – A Family Saga, a new political family drama by the British Nigerian writer Oladipo Agboluaje, will have its world premiere in the Dorfman theatre, directed by Lucian Msamati and starring Uzo Aduba.

Among the season’s other new work is Mr Loverman, Natasha Gordon’s stage adaptation of Bernardine Evaristo’s acclaimed novel about a married Caribbean man confronting his sexuality. Gary Beadle, Jo Martin and Danny Sapani are among the initial cast, with Paulette Randall directing.
There is also a new British musical, Glorious Madness, featuring songs by Joan Armatrading, with a book by Iman Qureshi and directed by Phyllida Lloyd.

The multi-award-winning theatre company Punchdrunk open a new immersive production called Ghostlight, conceived and directed by founder and artistic director Felix Barrett and curated by writer Lucy Kirkwood.

The programme is not without established works, but the balance is notable. Rather than a season dominated by Shakespeare and the traditional theatrical canon, the National has announced a series of modern classics and 20th-century works: West Side Story, co-directed by Marianne Elliott and Miranda Cromwell; Tennessee Williams’ Suddenly Last Summer, directed by Michael Grandage and starring Emma Corrin and Harriet Walter; David Hare’s Plenty, directed by former National Theatre director Richard Eyre and starring Emilia Clarke; and Death of a Salesman, starring Paul Mescal and Tracy Letts.
Tom Murphy’s A Whistle in the Dark and Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead will also return to the stage, with Mescal leading a repertory production alongside Death of a Salesman.

Notably, however, there is no Shakespeare production among the National’s three main stages in the new season. Hamlet will instead be among new titles added to the National Theatre Collection, the organisation’s streaming and education service.

blocks.caption: The National’s director Indhu Rubasingham and Kate Varah, the theatre’s executive. Varah said the theatre had invested in ‘bold artistic voices’. Photograph: Adama Jalloh

blocks.text: The National says the 2027 programme will include 18 productions, eight of them world premieres, alongside touring productions and work reaching audiences through cinema, streaming and schools.
Rubasingham said the season was united by “themes of resilience and hope” and was intended to reflect “the international spirit at the heart of our National Theatre”.

Kate Varah, the theatre’s executive and co-chief executive, said the programme represented an investment in “original storytelling” and in “bold artistic voices”, at a time when theatre was increasingly reaching audiences beyond its South Bank stages.

articles.title: Enact Trew’s law to automatically review ‘bent copper’ convictions, says report
articles.summary:
Experts say failure to immediately review cases involving corrupt police officers risks ‘ruining’ more lives

Convictions that imprisoned police officers were involved in obtaining should be…

blocks.text: Convictions that imprisoned police officers were involved in obtaining should be automatically reviewed to correct miscarriages of justice such as those perpetrated by the corrupt and racist officer DS Derek Ridgewell, a report says.

The proposed Trew’s law, named after Winston Trew – who was framed by Ridgewell and spent decades fighting to clear his name – would trigger an immediate, independent review of past cases linked to any jailed officer in England and Wales.

Ridgewell’s story has been described as “the real Line of Duty”, with reference to the BBC show about “bent coppers”. Since 2018, 13 victims of Ridgewell, including the Oval Four and members of the Stockwell Six had their convictions quashed. A 14th case involving the British Transport Police (BTP) officer was referred to the court of appeal in February.

Trew, who is working on the campaign for a new law with the miscarriages of justice charity Appeal, said: “When my convictions were finally quashed in 2019, it came after nearly 50 years of fighting to clear my name. No one should have to spend decades uncovering the truth about police wrongdoing. Justice shouldn’t depend on luck, or on victims fighting for years to expose miscarriages of justice. Trew’s law would place responsibility where it belongs: with the state.”

In 1980, Ridgewell was jailed for seven years for stealing mailbags worth £364,000, but an immediate review of his past cases was not initiated. In 2024, Lucy D’Orsi, chief constable of BTP, called the force’s failure to do so “simply inexcusable”.

Dr Joanna Gilmore, from the University of York, which produced the report with Appeal, said that despite D’Orsi’s apology “when we began researching this issue, we were struck by how little exists in law today to prevent history from repeating itself”.

She added: “In many of the cases we examined, judges noted in sentencing remarks how officers had used their police position to facilitate serious offending – and yet the decision to review their past cases remains discretionary, opaque, and unpredictable.”
CPS guidance recognises that a review may be required where a witness, including a police officer, is later “discredited” – but does not mandate it.

The researchers found that between 2023 and 2026, at least 64 current or former police officers received immediate custodial sentences for offences including serious dishonesty, physical and sexual violence, and abuse of position.
They also discovered that there was no central system to record when police officers received custodial sentences, nor whether their past cases were reviewed and, if so, the outcomes.

Dr Mattia Pinto, from the University of York, said: “Even today it is far too common for the lives of innocent people to be completely ruined by convictions based on unchecked evidence from corrupt officers.”
A triage process would focus on cases where the officer’s integrity was central to the conviction, while excluding purely administrative or peripheral involvement.

As well as triggering an immediate review, Trew’s law would require affected individuals to be notified and given disclosure where a material risk to conviction safety was identified, to enable timely access to legal advice.
Materiality includes providing witness evidence, preparing key investigative documents, or handling exhibits and disclosure.

Matt Foot, co-director of Appeal, said: “The criminal justice system takes far too long to correct miscarriages of justice. In the case of the victims of DS Ridgewell and his squads, it has taken an eternity. I believe there are many more victims out there still. It’s high time for Trew’s law so that officers that are doing harm who are imprisoned have their files investigated immediately to stop delay for those that have suffered enough.”

The campaign launch will be held in south London on Thursday night at Lambeth town hall, where an event was held in 1973 protesting against the imprisonment of the Oval Four. They were beaten up and framed for attempted theft and assaulting the police on the London Underground.
The Ministry of Justice has been approached for comment.

articles.title: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
articles.summary:
In two-hour address, president asked voters to ‘pretend that I’m on the ballot’ despite being deeply unpopular among electorate

Donald Trump said every adult citizen in the US will receive a…

blocks.text: Donald Trump said every adult citizen in the US will receive a dividend of $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, while delivering a historically long convention speech in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as radical communists and defended his unpopular war in Iran.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, claiming the payment was possible “because of our tremendous strength and success economically”.

Trump made the pledge, almost immediately raised ethical concerns, during a nearly two-hour long speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event.

Speaking in Dallas, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but much of his speech also focused on fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate in November.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”

The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in close races skipped the convention entirely.

Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good.

“So I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said. “Just one more time. Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago.”

In the build up to the midterm convention there had been something of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before switching to Wednesday, but the change wasn’t updated until Wednesday afternoon. There were also signs of a lack of enthusiasm among the rank and file.

Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long crowds to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech.
Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full.
“Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump said. This was not observed by Guardian reporters.

The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention underway, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page.

Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night. There was no risk of him falling asleep as he cracked jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year.

“He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.”

He attacked Democratic opponents with harsher words, focusing on senate candidate James Talarico in Texas, who will face Paxton, and former Republican governor Roy Cooper in North Carolina, who is now running for Senate.
The rest of the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda.

Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight.
Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10.
Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump.

“One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.”

Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches.
Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much more brief, while JD Vance, the vice-president, is expected to deliver the keynote.

articles.title: Doctor admits 'unusual' setup in Martin Romualdez's hospital confinement
articles.summary: The doctor who admitted Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez to Cardinal Santos Medical Center said Thursday that something was unusual in the lawmaker's confinement at the hospital.
articles.byline: LLANESCA T. PANTI, MAKI PULIDO, GMA News

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 11:57am
The doctor who admitted Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez to Cardinal Santos Medical Center said Thursday that something was unusual in the lawmaker's confinement at the hospital.

Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan made the statement during the hearing on Romualdez's motion for continued confinement at Cardinal Santos amid a P7.4 billion plunder case he is facing over his alleged links to the flood control mess.

Sibayan told the Sandiganbayan Third Division that while he was the admitting physician when Romualdez arrived at 4 p.m. in Cardinal Santos on September 7, he was not allowed to conduct any medical examination on the former House speaker.
"We were advised that we were not allowed inside the patient's (Romualdez) room," he said.
He said the instruction was relayed to him by attending physicians of Romualdez, Dr. Rody Sy and Dr. Rosalio Torres.
Asked by Associate Justice Ronald Moreno if such prohibition is unusual, Sibayan answered in the affirmative.
He added that Romualdez did not go to the emergency room but headed straight to a hospital room.
Not an emergency case
He also said that the current ailments of Romualdez are not an emergency case, although he remains at high risk of a heart attack.
"No," Sibayan said when asked by Moreno if Romualdez's case was an emergency case.
Sibayan also said that Romualdez had been complaining of chest pain ahead of his confinement.
When Dr. Torres took the stand, he said that one of the staff members of Romualdez informed him that the latter complained of chest pains around 9 a.m. on September 7.
"I advised that he be confined to look into this problem," he said.
Torres also testified that he believes Romualdez should remain detained in Cardinal Santos because the lawmaker is at "high risk of possible heart attack."
"In case of emergency, he would have an hour [to be treated]. We believe he may not be afforded that one hour [if he is transferred to another facility]," he said.
When Moreno asked what requires Romualdez's continued confinement, Torres said unstable angina with underlying coronary disease. He said it is an impending heart attack.
Torres also mentioned mental problems during Associate Justice Karl Miranda’s clarificatory questions. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
articles.summary: The US president gave a wide-ranging speech at the Republican midterm convention. He defended the war in Iran, trade wars and tariffs, and the White House ballroom. He also called Democrats evil and…

image.caption: Trump asked voters to 'pretend' that his name was on the ballot at the upcoming midterm electionsImage: Callaghan O'Hare/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump made a pitch to voters on Wednesday: a $5,000 (€4,300) "dividend" for every American adult if the Republican Party keeps control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.

"If the Republicans win ​the House of Representatives ​and ‌the United States Senate, both of them ... because of ‌our tremendous strength and success ‌economically, ​I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the ​United States of America for $5,000," Trump said at the ⁠Republican midterm ​convention on Wednesday.

"The only caveat we have is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America," he added. "We don't want you going to Canada spending the money, we don't want you going to China or Germany."

The president did not say how he would finance the measure, nor how the government would track where citizens spend the funds. He had previously promised citizens $2,000 checks from tariff revenues that have so far not materialized.
What else did Trump talk about?
Trump made the announcement as the two-day event kicked off in Dallas, Texas.

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump talked up some of the biggest — and most divisive — aspects of his second term in office, including the crackdown on immigration, the war in Iran, tariffs and subsequent economic retaliation, the White House ballroom, and restrictions on transgender people.
The president told voters to "pretend” that he's on the ballot at the elections that will see new representatives and senators elected in November.

blocks.caption: Trump joked about renaming a third body of water from the Strait of Hormuz to 'Trump Strait'Image: Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS

blocks.text: His attempts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario after America were met with rapturous applause. Later, he riffed on renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait."
Who else was at the Republican convention?
Other speakers focused less on the Trump administration's track record and instead attacked Democrats as "evil," "communists" and "socialists."

Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race against rising Democratic challenger James Talarico, who represents a younger and more progressive wing of that party.
Another Republican senator, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, was introduced by his Democratic counterpart, John Fetterman, in an unusual move.

Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with Democratic Party positions in recent years, introduced the Republican as his "great friend" and pledged to work with Trump to protect the state's steel industry.

blocks.caption: Senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, made the highly unusual move of giving a video message at the Republican conventionImage: Kent Nishimura/AFP

blocks.text: Conservative activists were also in attendance.

The Associated Press spotted Stewart Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers extremist group. Rhodes had been sentenced to 18 years in prison for his role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the US Capitol, but later benefited from Trump's sweeping clemency after he returned to office.
Trump also praised Erika Kirk for being in attendance on the eve of the one-year anniversary of the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk.
Vice President JD Vance received a brief shoutout near the end of the speech.

articles.title: Cayetano siblings traveled out of PH, BI confirms
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano both traveled out of the country, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed on Thursday, September 10. The Cayetano siblings were…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano both traveled out of the country, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed on Thursday, September 10.
The Cayetano siblings were reportedly spotted boarding a flight to Singapore and arriving at Changi Airport a few hours later on Wednesday evening.
“The Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirms that Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano are currently out of the country,” the BI said in a statement.
It added: “Based on BI records, there were no hold departure orders or derogatory records against the two senators, as of departure date, that would legally prevent them from leaving the country.”

The Office of the Ombudsman previously ordered Alan Cayetano, along with Sen. Robin Padilla, to respond to obstruction of justice charges over their alleged involvement in assisting fugitive-at-large Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa in going into hiding.
Dela Rosa is facing a crime against humanity charge before the International Criminal Court for his alleged role in the drug war, but his arrest warrant has yet to be served as he remains in hiding.

The Ombudsman has likewise received evidence from Sen. Panfilo Lacson regarding supposed “ghost” infrastructure and reclamation projects in Taguig, some of which were reportedly inserted into the budget by Cayetano himself.
Cayetanos’ flight an issue?
In a social media post, Lacson said the Cayetanos’ flight is a non-issue.
“This is not an issue as of the moment. Let’s make him (them) take a break from the stress caused by issues that he himself created,” Lacson remarked.
Meanwhile, both Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto said that senators’ personal trips don’t require permission from the chamber.
“Pag personal trips, hindi na kailangan mag abiso ang mga senador,” Gatchalian told the media in a text message.
(Senators no longer need to notify for personal trips.)
In a separate message, Sotto said: “Senators are not compelled to ask permission to leave the country.”/dl
