articles.title: What will Trump's retaliatory tariffs do to Canada’s economy big picture? Not that much, economists predict
articles.summary: With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on…

image.caption: Economists say this week's retaliation in the trade war will hurt some sectors and dent business confidence, but the sheer impact on the economy will be negligible. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on business owners' confidence.
Real hit will be indirect, economists warn — as some businesses likely to feel relief, others 'horrified'
The White House fired another shot in the Canada-U.S. trade war this week, banning outright the imports of Canadian dairy, motorcycles and some alcohol products.
But how much will those bans, along with fresh 50 per cent tariffs on a slate of other products, actually impact the Canadian economy?
Not all that much, say economists who’ve run the numbers. But that doesn't mean it won't hurt certain industries — and it certainly won't give business owners any peace of mind.

On Tuesday night, the White House retaliated against Canada's counter-tariffs with the bans and the addition of 50 per cent tariffs to items including mattresses and some paper products. American officials also dropped tariffs on others, such as toilet paper, cement and sugar.

But according to one analysis from Derek Holt, vice president and head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, the new tariffs will apply to an estimated $3 billion worth of Canadian goods, while the removed tariffs apply to about $2 billion worth — making the difference marginal, given Canada exported more than $527 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2025.

items: Trump banning import of Canadian booze, motorcycles, other goods into U.S.

blocks.text: The bans on alcohol, dairy and motorcycles will also be negligible, Holt adds, as Canada sends very little dairy and few motorcycles south of the border. Alcohol exports are a bit higher than the other categories, with $550 million worth sent to the U.S. last year, according to his analysis, but the export bans would still only impact $700 million worth of Canadian exports to the U.S.
"These actions are face saving by the U.S. administration, not substantive in nature and that’s a positive," Holt said in a note to investors on Wednesday.
How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?

He says the rising cost of oil — which soared past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday due to escalating tensions in the Middle East — poses a greater economic risk than the new U.S. measures.

At BMO, chief economist Doug Porter agrees. His team puts the value of newly tariffed items and those taken off the list both at about $2 billion, putting the country "in the same spot" as it was before the announcement.
But where the tariffs do hit, in certain industries or parts of the country, they will still hurt business owners badly, Porter told CBC News.

items: Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about shopping in the age of the Canada-U.S. trade dispute? Send us your questions before our Sept. 12 show.

blocks.text: "It's extremely negative for the new industries and products that were selected, but of course, some pretty important ones were taken off the list," he said.
"So there are going to be some relieved industries today and some horrified."
50% tariffs already an effective ban

For makers of Canadian booze, further escalation isn't a positive sign. Cal Bricker, CEO of Spirits Canada, says Canada exports much of the alcohol it makes to the U.S., making the continued targeting of his industry a concern.
U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says
But because many alcohol products already faced 50 per cent tariffs, upping the ante to a ban might not make a material difference to many booze producers.
Matt Johnston of craft brewer Collective Arts in Hamilton, Ont., says he wouldn't have been able to send any more of his beer south at a 50 per cent rate anyway.
"The reality is that once you add 50 per cent tariffs, it becomes extremely difficult to try and sell on the market.”

He already sent months worth of product to the U.S. before the new tariffs came into effect a few weeks ago, in hopes a deal could be reached before supplies ran out. Now, the plan is to grow the business within Canada and other international markets to make up for the loss of U.S. sales, where a fifth of their business used to come from.
"The world's a big place and we can look elsewhere," Johnston said.

As with alcohol, many of the banned items were already facing 50 per cent tariffs, RBC economist Nathan Janzen points out, which would have effectively kept them out of the U.S. market, meaning the impact of the ban will be relatively small.
Real hit will be indirect
Even if the impact will be small by the numbers, Tu Nguyen, an economist at accounting firm RSM Canada, says the escalation is still very real in terms of the message it sends to business owners.

While the U.S. has historically increased the tariff percentages in order to turn up the heat on Canada, Nguyen says an all-out ban signals a departure from that strategy. She says the real hit from the escalating retaliation will be indirect — the tit for tat denting business confidence.
"A lot of these tariffs, they sound really big … but they don't hit the economy nearly as badly as one would think," Nguyen said.
“The bigger hit, I would say … comes from uncertainty.”

And unlike in the past, when the U.S. gave many weeks or months of lead time before tariffs went into effect, some of the newly announced measures will come into force as soon as next week. Nguyen says this gives businesses less time to prepare or pivot to new markets, and introduces another worry for business owners on both sides of the border.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Shawn Benjamin

articles.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
articles.summary: Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the…

image.caption: Google has signed a deal to purchase half of the energy produced at the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant over the next 22 yearsImage: Anne Kauranen/REUTERS

blocks.text: US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.
Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.
Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.
Why communities are fighting AI data centers
Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.
The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."
Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."
The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.
Resources under pressure
Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.
Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.
"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.
Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.
AI under pressure: scams, security and sustainability

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.summary:
Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which

blocks.text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.

“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.

The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.

Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.

In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.

Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel Noboa  Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.

During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.

Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

articles.title: Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war
articles.summary: Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his vow to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an…

image.caption: The NFL's Buffalo Bills say the Canadian national anthem will be played alongside the U.S. national anthem at the team's home opener on Sept. 13 against the Detroit Lions. (Adrian Kraus/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his vow to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an unexpected announcement.
NFL team says O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed Sept. 17

Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his plan to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an unexpected announcement.

On Wednesday, the team said on social media platform X that both O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed before its Sept. 17 home opener against the Detroit Lions, the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium.

The Bills announced that "for the first time in Highmark Stadium history, we will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame." Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho will perform the American anthem and Toronto band Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada.

items: 'Unhinged' for Canada to call dispute with U.S. a trade war, says Trump's tariff chief

blocks.text: In Buffalo, the Canadian national anthem is rarely heard before NFL games, but it's commonly played before NHL games, even when the Sabres are up against American opponents. In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.

items: #TheMoment Buffalo Sabres fans sang O Canada after a mic failed

blocks.text: Buffalo is the only U.S.-based NHL team that plays both national anthems before home games against American and Canadian teams.
Tit-for-tat tariffs escalate trade war

On Tuesday, Trump signed five proclamations to ban Canadian imports including alcohol, motorcycles and various other products to the U.S. as of Sept. 29, and slap 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products starting next week.
The latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. comes after Canadian retaliatory tariffs, promised after trade talks fell apart last month, came into force Tuesday.

In explaining why Canada chose not to sign a trade deal amid Trump's deep tariffs on billions in Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries."
Bills owners Terry and Kim Pegula bought the team for $1.4 billion US from the estate of late Hall of Fame owner Ralph Wilson in 2014.

Jozy Altidore, a former U.S. National Team soccer player, MLS champion and Toronto FC star, was also among the new limited partners announced.
It marked the first time in franchise history that minority owners were added.

articles.title: Off to India, Marcos first PH leader to attend BRICS summit
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will become the first Philippine leader to attend a BRICS Summit when he travels to India this week, joining the bloc’s annual gathering in his capacity as…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will become the first Philippine leader to attend a BRICS Summit when he travels to India this week, joining the bloc’s annual gathering in his capacity as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) for 2026.

Marcos will attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12 to 13 at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to the spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Assistant Secretary Annalyn Ratonel, on Wednesday.
Manila sees the summit as a strategic opportunity to engage the major economies making up BRICS, which account for a major share of global output and trade.
Alternative to West

BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the core members of the group. It’s expanded membership now stands at 11 after the inclusion of Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates.
It currently has 10 partner countries: Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.

The first BRICS Summit was held in 2009. All together, the grouping accounts for 49.5 percent of the world population, 40 percent of the global gross domestic product, and 26 percent of international trade.
BRICS is largely seen as offering emerging economies an alternative to Western-dominated alliances or institutions.
“Building a dialogue between Asean led by the Philippines and BRICS led by India could create significant geopolitical and economic support,” Ratonel said on Wednesday.
Making follow-ups
“This can create synergies between the priorities of Asean and BRICS that can lead to economic opportunities, trade diversification, regional security, and support for climate resilience,” she added.

According to the DFA, while Manila’s engagement with BRICS would be anchored on Asean centrality, “we recognize the value of working alongside international partners to address pressing global issues and challenges.”

The President will be accompanied at the summit by first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, as well as Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda and Finance Secretary Frederick Go.
Engage when appropriate
He is scheduled to meet with Indian business leaders to strengthen economic relations and follow up on commitments made by Indian companies during his visit to India in August last year.
Following that trip, President Marcos announced $5.8 billion worth of investment pledges from Indian companies covering technology, health, energy and infrastructure.

Marcos is also scheduled to have a bilateral meeting with Modi to discuss the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and review the implementation of the two countries’ Five-Year Plan of Action for 2025 to 2029.
Trade and investment, agriculture, climate change, defense and security, and science and technology are among the areas that could be discussed, Ratonel said.

Asked whether possible Philippine membership in the bloc would be discussed as well, Ratonel said the matter would require “further study” but that the country would continue to monitor developments and engage with BRICS when appropriate.
“We would also follow the experiences of our fellow Asean countries that are members (or partners) of BRICS,” he said, apparently referring to Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand. /cb

articles.title: This is deep: Hungary’s grave-digging contest
articles.summary: NYERGESUJFALU, Hungary — Like death itself, this was no joke. A grave-digging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38…

blocks.text: NYERGESUJFALU, Hungary — Like death itself, this was no joke.
A grave-digging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38 competitors grabbed picks and shovels on Saturday.
The Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators organizes the contest to showcase the grave-digging trade and its skills, and shake off death-related taboos.

The dry summer-baked soil in the public cemetery in Nyergesújfalu, northern Hungary, proved a worthy adversary for the 19 two-man teams. They huffed and puffed and sweated as they raced for the title of quickest-dug and most stylish grave.
‘Beautifully carved’
“Speed is the main thing here, not the beauty,” said Róbert Nagy, the victor with his teammate László Kiss.
“When you have to dig a grave for a funeral, you have to be very careful about the exact dimensions and to make sure that it is beautifully carved.”
Their winning time was 1 hour, 21 minutes, digging to contest specifications of graves 1.6 meters (5½ feet) deep, 2 meters (6½ feet) long and 0.8 meters (2.6 feet) wide.
They shared a cash prize of 200,000 Hungarian forints (about $640). /cb

articles.title: Human Rights Tribunal orders B.C. doctor to pay after refusing to provide trans teen with puberty blocker shot
articles.summary: A B.C. family doctor has been ordered to pay $28,100, after refusing to inject a transgender teen with a prescribed hormone blocker, citing religious and cultural reasons.

image.caption: The B.C. Human Rights Tribunal office is pictured in Vancouver on March 27, 2023. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A B.C. family doctor has been ordered to pay $28,100, after refusing to inject a transgender teen with a prescribed hormone blocker, citing religious and cultural reasons.
Family doctor Henry Ajaero said he was 'uncomfortable and unprepared' to provide shot of Lupron
A B.C. family doctor has been ordered to pay $28,100 after refusing to inject a transgender teen with a prescribed hormone blocker, citing religious and cultural reasons.
Dr. Henry Ajaero, who has run a family practice in Delta since 2014, was ordered to pay the compensation in a Sept. 1 B.C. Human Rights decision, which found his conduct was discriminatory.

In March 2021, Ajaero told a transgender teen and her mother who made an appointment at his practice that he would not inject a prescribed medication called Lupron, saying "he did not feel comfortable administering it."
Ajaero argued to the tribunal that he did not administer the injection because "doing so would go against his religious beliefs" and "because it is outside the scope of his practice."
The tribunal ruled he failed to establish a conflict between his religious beliefs and the medical services the teen was seeking.

"Dr. Ajaero has not established that either the Religion Standard or the Expertise Standard were reasonably necessary to achieve their purposes. This is likely because they were developed quickly, in the context of a busy and stressful day, with incomplete information," the decision reads in part.

items: Why this American doctor is leaving Utah to serve a remote community in B.C.

blocks.text: "This context is an explanation for Dr. Ajaero’s decision, but it does not justify his decision to deny medical services to a vulnerable trans youth because of her gender identity."
Refusal to administer
The decision describes Child Q, the 14-year-old at the centre at the decision, as a "brave, sensitive, kind transgender girl."

It says in late 2020, she came out as transgender and struggled with her mental health as she entered puberty. Ajaero referred her to the B.C. Gender Clinic, where an endocrinologist prescribed Lupron, a medication that pauses puberty.
According to the decision, Child Q describes the day she started the medication as "one of the best days of my life."
Lupron needs to be injected every three to four weeks. It can be injected at home, but according to the decision, Child Q and her family preferred to have it done by a doctor.
Her first appointment to get an injection at her family doctor's was March 5.
The decision said when Ajaero learned that the shot was Lupron, he told Child Q's mother he would not be administering it.

items: Regulator suspends B.C. Realtor's licence, cites 'urgent circumstances'

blocks.text: "He explained this was for religious and cultural reasons, and he hoped that was OK. Mother Q said it was not OK."

Ajaero's charting notes from the appointment said: "I noticed that the injection is for gender re-assignment as patient is already in the waiting room with [her] mother. I called mother into the room and explained to her that I would not be able to give the injection. Based on my religious belief and cultural background."
Child Q and her mother never spoke with Ajaero again outside of legal proceedings.

The decision found that "while it is true that Lupron was prescribed through the Gender Clinic, and was intended to give Child Q time to consider options relating to her gender identity, it is not medication for gender re-assignment."
"It does not, on its own, conflict with Dr. Ajaero’s stated religious belief that 'God created man and woman.'"
'Uncomfortable and unprepared'

The decision said Ajaero attended medical school in Nigeria, and practised medicine in Nigeria, South Africa, and rural B.C. before opening his clinic in Delta. It says he is Christian and "his religion is an important part of his life."

Ajaero said he has around 2,800 to 2,900 patients, and works five days per week, seeing about 50 patients per day. The decision notes that at the time of the incident, Ajaero was under particular strain due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

"He testified that he had never interacted with a trans person (to his knowledge) or been involved in any 'gender therapy.' He had never administered Lupron for any purpose. It was apparent from his evidence that, in all the circumstances, he felt uncomfortable and unprepared," read the decision.

items: B.C. Human Rights Tribunal orders Best Buy to pay fired employee over $60K

blocks.text: "I accept that these feelings motivated his decision to deny services to Child Q, and were not based on an intention to discriminate against her."
Ajaero applied to limit the publication of information that could identify him and his clinic, arguing in part that doctors who provide gender affirming care have faced threats.
The tribunal denied that application, saying there is no evidence that doctors who refuse to give gender-affirming care face the same risk.
"I am not prepared to assume that the public response is the same to doctors on both sides of the issue," the decision states.

articles.title: Government exempts interprovincial pipelines from review by impact assessment agency
articles.summary: The federal government is moving ahead with changes that will exempt a number of energy projects from a layer of its environmental assessment process.

image.caption: Workers lay pipe during construction of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion in Abbotsford, B.C., in 2023. The federal government is exempting projects like interprovincial pipelines from a portion of its regulatory review process. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government is moving ahead with changes that will exempt a number of energy projects from a layer of its environmental assessment process.
Projects will be reviewed by energy regulator as part of move to streamline approval

Projects including pipelines and transmission lines that cross international or provincial borders, as well as offshore renewable energy projects, will no longer be subject to an environmental review by the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC), according to the new regulations published in the Canada Gazette on Wednesday.
Instead, those projects will be solely reviewed by the Canada Energy Regulator (CER).

"The CER has expertise conducting impact assessments that review a project's effects on a range of environmental factors, including air, water, soil, climate change, wildlife, species at risk and Canada's environmental obligation," a government news release said.
Certain oilsands extraction projects and fossil fuel-fired power generating projects are also being removed from the list of projects that will be subject to IAAC review, the news release said.
Major projects to get only one environmental assessment as Ottawa, Quebec strike deal
"These projects and facilities will continue to be subject to equally robust applicable provincial and federal assessment processes," the release reads.
Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the changes are "great news" for industry.

"It does not mean these projects will not have environmental assessment — it means the [IAAC] will not duplicate some types of projects the provincial governments or the Canadian Energy Regulator (pipelines and transmission) are already assessing," she wrote in a post on X.
A 'wrecking ball' to regulations: environmental group
The changes come after Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to streamline regulatory approvals for major projects during the last election.

The Liberals, with the help of the Conservatives, passed Bill C-5 shortly after the 2025 election. That legislation allows the government to fast-track major projects it deems to be in the national interest. But these changes will impact the reviews for other major projects that don't receive that designation.
The government first proposed the changes as part of a suite of measures in May and subsequently launched consultations on the proposed reforms that wrapped up in July.

items: Danielle Smith wants to double Alberta oil production. Can she bring back the boom?
As Carney advances Metro Vancouver port expansion, environmentalists raise concern for at-risk species
Proposed changes to endangered species law would 'stab it to death,' says scientist

blocks.text: The report on those consultations was published on Tuesday, the same day the regulatory changes were announced.
"There was no forewarning of this decision," said Julia Levin of the Environmental Defence advocacy group in a statement.
"Prime Minister Carney has once again taken a wrecking ball to Canada's environmental safeguards and climate progress."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: BARMM 2026 elections: Frequently Asked Questions
articles.summary: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will hold its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026.

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will hold its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026.
Here are the frequently asked questions that can help you understand the elections:
What is the relevance of the BARMM elections?
The election paves the way for the transition of the region's interim government under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) to an elected regional administration.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. described it as the “fruition of an entire peace process that began in 1968, then to the Tripoli Agreement, and then the BARMM," as he called on Filipinos to protect and strengthen the gains of the country's peace process.
When will the Bangsamoro parliamentary election be held?
The first BARMM parliamentary elections will be on September 14, 2026.
The election period runs from July 16 until September 29, 2026.
Meanwhile, the campaign period is from July 30 to September 12, 2026.
How many registered voters are there in BARMM?
There are 2.393 million registered voters in the Bangsamoro region.
During the final command conference in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman George Garcia said he is hoping for a 65-70% voter turnout in the BARMM polls.
How many voting precincts are there in the BARMM?
There are 5,212 voting precincts in 105 municipalities and two cities in the Bangsamoro Region.
To help voters locate their voting precincts, the Comelec launched its Precinct Finder on September 7.
They can locate their voting precinct by entering their full name, date of birth, and place of registration.
What time can voters begin to cast their votes?
Senior citizens, persons with disabilities, and pregnant voters will be allowed to vote as early as 5 a.m., while regular voting hours begin at 7 a.m.
Voting will continue until 7 p.m. to ensure all qualified voters can cast their ballots.
How many election areas of concern are there?
There are 108 election areas of concern (EACs) in the Bangsamoro region: Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Tawi-Tawi, and special areas of concern.
Of the total EACs, 15 areas were placed in the Green category, 39 are under Yellow category, 27 under Orange, and another 27 under Red.
According to Comelec, areas under the green category have no security concerns or are relatively peaceful and orderly.

Areas under the yellow category are those with suspected election-related incidents (ERIs) in the last two elections, politically motivated ERIs during the current election period, intense partisan rivalry, or a history of being placed under COMELEC control.
Areas under the orange category meet two or more under the yellow category or exhibit serious armed threats.

Areas under the red category have one or more factors identified under the yellow and/or orange categories, along with serious armed threats or the existence of any ground for the declaration of COMELEC control.
How many seats are in the BARMM parliamentary government?
There are 80 seats in the Bangsamoro parliamentary government.
Of the total seats, 40 are designated for party representatives, 32 are for district representatives, and eight are for sectoral representatives.

There are nine seats for Lanao del Sur, five each for Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, four each for Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, three for Cotabato City, and two for the Special Geographic Area.
For the sectoral groups, two seats are for non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, two for settler communities, abd one each for women, youth, traditional leaders and ulama.
In August, the NMIPs selected two representatives for the Bangsamoro Parliament.
The selected NMIP representatives are Jo Genna Jover from the Teduray indigenous peoples and Leticio Datuwata from the Lambangian indigenous groups.
They will be proclaimed along with the winning candidates after the elections.
How does the BARMM government work?
In the Bangsamoro region, the legislative power is vested in the Bangsamoro Parliament, while the executive power is given to the Chief Minister.

Meanwhile, the judicial power is excercised by in the Supreme Court, as well as in the Shari’ah and regular courts within the Bangsamoro territorial jurisdiction that form part of the Philippine judicial system. —Mariel Celine Serquina/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
articles.summary: Declassified documents show Spanish and Moroccan authorities were alerted to social media calls for a mass migrant crossing the day before tens of thousands entered Ceuta.

blocks.text: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.
The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.
On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.
Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".

The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades".
It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.

The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.
Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.
However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.
Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".
But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.ed
"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.
Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".
The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.
Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".

A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".
Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.
"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

articles.title: Ex-Doctor Who actor Noel Clarke charged with several sexual offences including assault, voyeurism
articles.summary: Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who from 2005 to 2010, has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown…

image.caption: British actor, writer and director Noel Clarke arrives at the High Court on March 7, 2025, in London, England. Clarke has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, that stem from allegations made by five women, U.K. prosecutors announced on Wednesday. (Getty Imag

blocks.text: Entertainment

Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who from 2005 to 2010, has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown Prosecution Service announced on Wednesday.
Charges stem from allegations made by 5 women against actor who was on BBC show from 2005-2010

Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who, has been charged with six sexual offences including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced on Wednesday.

The British actor and filmmaker, who is 50 and rose to fame after playing Mickey Smith on the BBC show from 2005 to 2010, also faces one charge of exposure and three charges of voyeurism. Under CPS, a voyeurism charge refers to when someone observes or records another person carrying out a private act without their consent, typically for sexual gratification.
According to CPS, the alleged offences involving Clarke took place between 2007 to 2016 and stem from allegations made by five women.

It also comes five years after a Guardian expose published sexual harrassment, groping and bullying claims made against Clarke by 20 women, including sources that alleged they were "sexually harassed or inappropriately" touched on set of Doctor Who — allegations the actor vehemently denied.
According to the Guardian, the recent charges were handed down after an investigation that began in September 2025.
Clarke is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Oct. 21.

The actor is also known for writing and starring in the teen crime drama films Kidulthood (2006), Adulthood (2008) and Brotherhood (2016), which explored drug abuse, bullying and violence on the streets of London. He also directed Adulthood and directed and produced Brotherhood.
His other on-screen credits include Centurion (2010), Fast Girls (2012), Star Trek Into Darkness (2013) and the TV series Bulletproof (2018-2021).
with files from Reuters

articles.title: Politics live: Kevin Rudd urges more multilateral diplomacy; UK hopeful Australia will join West Bank trade ban
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Don’t appease One Nation on migration warns Malinauskas

The wickedly popular South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas,…

blocks.text: Don’t appease One Nation on migration, Malinauskas warns
The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has iwarned the Albanese government not to join the “madness” of cutting migration to appease One Nation.

In a speech in Sydney last night, Malinauskas – whose grandparents migrated to Australia after the second world war – said the wave of populist politics has “more than arrived in Australia”, but the government should push back.

double quotation markAbove all else, [we must] preserve our strong migration program … The correct political response to anti-immigration politics and populists is not appeasement. More troubling is the prospect of mainstream politics entering a political race to the bottom for who can cut migration numbers the most. This is not unfortunate – this is madness. There could be no greater act of national economic self harm at this time than to slash migration numbers for political purposes.
He also warns against cutting international student numbers, calling it “crazy”.

double quotation markImagine if we did this to the mining industry, there world be an ad on every television station and mobile phone about how we’re killing the goose that lays the golden egg. It is crazy.

blocks.caption: Peter Malinauskas. Photograph: Sia Duff/The Guardian

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18m agoDon’t appease One Nation on migration, Malinauskas warns
42m agoAustralia should ‘put shoulder to the wheel’ on multilateral diplomacy: Rudd

blocks.text: ‘We need to explain Australia doesn’t have a migration crisis’: Malinauskas

Peter Malinaukas says he understands the concerns of Australians worried about migration and the housing shortage in Australia, but that the answer is politicians need to explain there is a housing crisis not a migration crisis happening.
He tells the ABC’s AM program that Australia will soon have more people over 65 than under 15 and migration will be essential to replace the ageing workforce.

double quotation markWe need to explain that Australia doesn’t really have a migration crisis so much as a housing crisis. If we have a housing crisis, we would do well to focus our skills policy on making sure that we’re bringing in the very workers that we require in the housing construction industry. You know, Australia’s got a massive shortage of almost every trade. Everyone, I think, accepts that it needs to be a well-calibrated, balanced migration program. My point is that we haven’t seen much evidence in the political discourse in this country in the last few years making the case for migration. Just to be seeing be a lot of culture wars being executed against migration. And I think that’s self-defeating, and we’ve got a responsibility to stand up against it.
But when asked what the magic number is for a well-balanced migration program, Malinauskas won’t say.

Instead of coming up with an arbitrary number and then cutting different parts of the migration program, Malinaukas says governments should work from the ground up, determining the skills shortages, and growth in regional areas and then coming up with a target.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the fortnight.

We’ll be hearing more on migration today with the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, overnight warning the Albanese government not to join the “race to the bottom” against One Nation in cutting migration. The premier is doing the media rounds this morning.
Speaking of One Nation, the stoush between Pauline Hanson and Andrew Hastie continues – we’ll be following that closely.

And expect some more fight over the grants program that gave Labor seats a majority of funding, as well as the government’s digital duty of care bill, it’ll be an interesting issue for the Coalition – we understand there’s a pretty wide spread in opinion across their party room over the bill.
There’s plenty to get to, so let’s get stuck in!

blocks.caption: Adeshola Ore

blocks.text: Adeshola Ore
Victoria has highest rate of car theft and home burglary claims in ICA data
Melbourne recorded more insurance claims for stolen and broken-into cars than all other Australian capital cities combined, according to data analysis by the Insurance Council of Australia.

Property crime data released by the ICA on Wednesday night showed Victoria had the highest rates of car theft and home burglary claims in the country in the last financial year. Analysis of Insurance Statistics Australia (ISA) data showed that there were more than 12,300 claims – costing insurers $244m – lodged in the state for cars stolen or broken into.
In the same time period, every other state and territory recorded a decline.
The ICA’s chief executive, Andrew Hall, said in Victoria a car was stolen or broken into every 43 minutes while a home is broken into every two hours.
double quotation markThe insurance data shows Victoria has a crime problem, and it is being felt directly by households, businesses and communities.

Before the November state election, the ICA called for the next state government to reduce car theft and property crime through a statewide strategy and better intelligence sharing, improve disaster recovery by establishing centrally coordinated clean-up arrangements, and ease cost-of-living pressures by abolishing stamp duty on business, home and contents insurance products.
It also called for improving insurance affordability for healthcare professionals, community organisations and live music venues by “modernising civil liability laws”.
It was ‘hoped’ Australia would join UK trade ban on Israeli settlements in West Bank: Emily Thornberry
The head of the UK’s foreign affairs select committee says there was hope Australia would join the UK’s trade ban on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Australia is preparing another round of sanctions against Israel but has stopped short of joining the UK’s trade ban. On Tuesday, the UK government announced it would ban imported goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30, Emily Thornberry, the chair of the UK’s foreign affairs select committee, was asked whether she hoped Australia would join the UK’s trade ban decision:
double quotation markI think it was hoped that they might but, you know, all countries have their own decisions to make. We all want the same thing and nobody says this is easy.
Thornberry said she had a “a lot of time” for the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong:

double quotation markI don’t know the basis upon which she’s made a decision not to be involved with us, but I’m sure that you know she believes that what she’s doing is in the interests of Palestinians and in the interests of justice.
She later added:
double quotation markI’m always happy to talk to my Australian friends and maybe even persuade them.

On Wednesday, Wong said she was concerned a blanket ban could have “unintended consequences” for Australian businesses, Palestinians and Israelis and reiterated the country would continue to protect the prospect of a two-state solution.

blocks.caption: Emily Thornberry in the House of Commons in London. Photograph: House of Commons/Reuters

blocks.text: Australia should ‘put shoulder to the wheel’ on multilateral diplomacy: Rudd

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd is in Canberra for a round of high-profile speeches this week, marking his return to Australia after serving as ambassador to Washington DC.
Rudd spoke at the Australian Institute of International Affairs on Wednesday night and will be at the National Press Club today.

He said Australia must continue to push multilateral diplomacy, even as Donald Trump withdraws the US from a range of important global institutions. Australia, as a leading middle power, should promote the United Nations system, which has support across Asia and Europe, according to Rudd.

double quotation markThere remains an opportunity for Australia, in partnership with other middle powers around the world, to put our shoulders to the wheel in supporting those UN multilateral institutions which now find themselves under financial and institutional pressure as a result of the US withdrawing. Australia remains active in the UN, the IMF and the World Bank. We remain active in the G20 and in APEC. We remain active in major regional institutions, such as the Pacific Islands Forum, where the government has once again registered a remarkable series of foreign policy achievements.
Rudd said this kind of serious engagement would “put flesh on the bones” of the plan outlined by the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at Davos earlier this year.

double quotation markAnd it would mark a deeply practical contribution to sustaining the multilateral rules-based system as America resolves its internal domestic debate on its future posture within it.
Good morning
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live coverage for Thursday.
Krishani Dhanji will join us shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Victoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimated
articles.summary:
Exclusive: State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 months

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Victorian government sat on a report for more than 12 months that found the state’s koala population was in chronically poor health.

The review of the state’s koala populations, led by state science agency the Arthur Rylah Institute in conjunction with scientists from major universities, was completed for the Victorian government in June 2025.

It estimated there were 217,000 koalas in the state in 2023 and 224,800 in 2024 – a dramatic drop from past estimates of 460,000, which the report attributed to different survey and modelling methodology, rather than an actual population decline.
As part of the research, scientists conducted health and disease assessments on 68 koalas, with 29 of the koalas (43%) found to be in such poor health they “were euthanised on welfare grounds”.
The report warned the surveys found “a higher-than-expected proportion of koalas from seven geographically distinct regions in a state of chronically poor health and welfare”.

The government published the report on Wednesday morning as the new environment minister, Jaclyn Symes, announced $2.6m for koala conservation, including for habitat restoration and research into koala health and genetics.
Leanne Wicker, a wildlife veterinarian who was one of the authors on the report, said researchers had been shocked by the poor health of some the koalas they found in the field.

“While we were doing this research we knew we were seeing something that urgently needed attention and understanding,” she said. “And it’s been very difficult to get the support and resources needed because the report hadn’t been made public.”

She said the overabundance of certain local Victorian koala populations – such as those at French Island and in western Victoria – had created a perception that the state’s overall koala population was thriving. “What we’ve missed is we have a crisis in our koala populations in Victoria because we have a very concerning level of poor health and welfare.”

Deakin University’s Desley Whisson, another author on the report, said while the 2024 population estimate of about 225,000 koalas “seems like a lot, most of those koalas are in areas where there are high densities of animals”.
“There’s large parts of the state where koalas occur at low densities and are probably in poor health,” she said.
She said the government needed to turn its attention to areas with low numbers “because we could be losing koalas in some parts of the state without even knowing”.

The report used systematic visual and acoustic surveys in 2023 and 2024 to monitor koalas at 182 sites. That data was then used to estimate the overall abundance and distribution of Victoria’s koala population.

The report states the drop in the estimated population from previous estimates of 460,000 was due to changes in the methodology used. It said the new data also represented the first time koala populations had been surveyed statewide.

Of the 68 koalas sampled for health and welfare checks, 39 healthy individuals were rereleased, with healthy animals present at all of the locations sampled, according to the report. But 29 koalas were euthanised due to ill health.

Koalas that were euthanised were more likely to have poor coat condition, dental disease, and “wet bottom” (an advanced urinary tract infection, most commonly caused by chlamydia), and were more likely to occur in areas with high koala densities. Dental disease was recorded in 37% of koalas across all life stages and regions, except Mallacoota, according to the report.
The report states that these findings raised concerns “for the health of Victorian koalas”.
after newsletter promotion

“Clinical signs consistent with chronic ill-health were observed across all life stages, suggesting that multiple individual, environmental and demographic stressors may be contributing to prolonged physiological stress within these populations,” the scientists wrote.
Animal Justice party MP, Georgie Purcell, said the research painted a grim picture of the health and wellbeing of Victoria’s koalas.

“It is clear that we need to use every lever possible to ensure they’re given the best chance at survival, or we will soon be just like the many states across Australia where koalas are listed as endangered,” she said.
The report also found that 23% of Victoria’s koala population now lived in the state’s blue gum plantation estate “where they occur at much higher density than koalas in neighbouring native forest”.
“Given the high estimated density of koalas within blue gum plantations, changes to the plantation estate size and/or stand ages may result in significant changes to population size,” it states.
Jessica Robertson, from advocacy group the Koala Alliance, called Wednesday’s funding announcement “a calculated political rescue mission for Labor, not for koalas”.
“Sitting on critical ecological data for over a year while koalas continued to suffer and disappear is a shocking failure of transparency and responsibility,” she said.
Guardian Australia sought comment from Symes.

A Victorian environment department spokesperson said since receiving the report it had been working with other agencies, and consulting external groups, “to prioritise actions and design projects that address its findings and recommendations”.
A spokesperson said Wednesday’s funding announcement was the result of this work.
The environment department’s spokesperson said the timing of the report’s public release had not affected “important work” the government was already doing to manage the health of the state’s koalas.

articles.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
articles.summary: A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been…

image.caption: The Ukrainian leader's plane arrived in Oslo on September 8Image: Frederik Ringnes/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone.

"His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa.
Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway.

Moldova's government spokesperson said later on Wednesday that the flight was delayed when the country's airspace was closed over a drone alert. The spokesperson said in a statement that Zelenskyy's plane was able to depart after a Russian drone came down on Moldovan territory.

The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald.

blocks.caption: At the funeral of the Norwegian King Harald V, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (center) was joined by other leadersImage: Dylan Martinez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russian drone in Moldova
Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident.
A claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday.
The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed.
However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store and the Moldovan government spokesperson.

articles.title: China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
articles.summary: A university professor is calling for English to no longer be taught as a graded core subject in Chinese schools. Opponents argue that, in a globalized world, knowing English is beneficial for the…

image.caption: Will these children still be graded in English during their high school graduation exams?Image: maginechina-Tuchong/IMAGO

blocks.text: From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities.
Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has.

"Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media.
China: Studying instead of Playing
English as a required subject starting in third grade

English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter.

"How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position.
He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so.
Why English? 'AI translates'
Tang's opinion spread quickly online.
"Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing.
Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam.

blocks.caption: Secondary schools in China end after 12th grade. These young people are headed to their final examImage: HPIC/picture alliance

blocks.text: Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers.
No English proficiency, no competitiveness

There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements.

Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life."

blocks.caption: In Saudi Arabia, Mandarin is the second foreign language taught at schools ― after EnglishImage: FAYEZ NURELDINE/AFP

blocks.text: Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history.

"Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions."

For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world.
Why Mandarin Chinese courses are growing in African schools
Little interest in language studies

Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity.
The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics.
Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty.
"Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time.

Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Guy Turcotte, who killed his 2 children, requesting temporary absence from prison
articles.summary: Guy Turcotte was sentenced to life in prison in 2015 after being convicted of second-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of his two young children.

image.caption: Guy Turcotte will appear before the Parole Board of Canada later this month. (Graham Hughes/CP)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Guy Turcotte was sentenced to life in prison in 2015 after being convicted of second-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of his two young children.
'I knew this day would come,' says Turcotte's ex, mother of murdered children
A former Quebec cardiologist who was convicted of second-degree murder in the 2009 stabbing deaths of his children is requesting a temporary release from prison.

Guy Turcotte was found guilty of killing his two young children — Olivier, 5, and Anne-Sophie, 3 — by an 11-person jury in 2015. He was subsequently sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 17 years.

Turcotte will appear before the Parole Board of Canada on Sept. 22 to request an escorted temporary absence, which allows an inmate to leave a correctional institution for a limited time, accompanied by a Correctional Service of Canada staff member.
Offenders can apply for an escorted temporary absence at any point during their sentence.
Isabelle Gaston, Turcotte's ex-wife and the children's mother, said she will read a letter at the hearing.
"I knew this day would come and I have been trying to prepare myself for a long time," she wrote in a social media post Wednesday.
"I choose to believe in the process, even though I have been disappointed countless times."
Parole board will consider multiple factors
Turcotte was initially found not criminally responsible for the children's death in a trial held in 2011.
At the time, his defence argued that Turcotte was suffering from mental illness that stemmed from his troubled marriage. He and Gaston were recently separated when he killed their children.
Escorted temporary releases may be granted for a variety of reasons, including medical, personal development or counselling, community service, family contact or on compassionate grounds.
The parole board will consider Turcotte’s conduct in prison, risk to reoffend, and proposed release plan when determining whether or not to grant his request.

items: Guy Turcotte found guilty of 2nd-degree murder in deaths of his 2 children
Guy Turcotte sentenced to life with no chance of parole for 17 years

blocks.text: In her social media post, Gaston said she hopes the hearing will be "be rigorous, prudent, and worthy of what Olivier and Anne-Sophie deserve."

"When a criminal act occurs, we are no longer just victims. We become, despite ourselves, representatives of society," she wrote, adding that that comes with a responsibility to ensure that justice is served with prudence and humanity.
"The same applies to a request for privileges."

articles.title: China to Teodoro: Stop the provocation, theatrics
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Chinese Foreign Ministry on Wednesday called on a “certain individual” to stop what they described as “provocations” and “threatrics” following Defense Secretary Gilberto…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Chinese Foreign Ministry on Wednesday called on a “certain individual” to stop what they described as “provocations” and “threatrics” following Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro’s public denunciation of China’s claims over the 2016 arbitral ruling at a defense forum in Seoul.

Chinese Foreign Ministry Mao Ning said that China’s position over the South China Sea arbitration remained “clear and consistent”, citing a similar statement written in the handwritten note delivered to Teodoro at the Seoul Defense Dialogue on Tuesday.

“We urge the certain individual of the Philippine side to cut the provocations and theatrics, and stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea,” she told reporters at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
She further asserted that the country’s arbitral case in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) was a “distortion and abuse” of its mandate.
The Unclos is an international treaty, which establishes a legal framework for maritime disputes.
In 2016, the arbitral tribunal ruled in favor of the Philippines, recognizing its 370-kilometer exclusive economic zone in the western region.

“The Philippines unilaterally initiated the case, which is a distortion and abuse of the Unclos dispute settlement mechanism. It is the Philippine side who has violated and undermined its integrity and authority,” she said.

She added that the country was the one violating and undermining the Unclos, which was a response to Teodoro’s remarks after he called out China for disrespecting the arbitral tribunal, as well as the international forum.
The defense chief, alongside other foreign defense leaders, attended the multilateral security forum in Korea.
During a question-and-answer portion after Teodoro’s speech at the event, a Chinese delegate delivered a letter to him, asserting China’s position in the South China Sea. /cb
