articles.title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
articles.summary: The Tetris Company says it takes "copyright infringement very seriously" and is not involved with the game.

blocks.text: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.
The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website.
On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".
The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown.
"At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game.
"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."

The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.
Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website.
"Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.
Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

articles.title: German chancellor accuses far-right AfD party of seeking ‘ethnic cleansing’
articles.summary: Friedrich Merz says Alternative für Deutschland is ‘dividing our society’ after party won nearly 44% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt state election

blocks.text: Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.

In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.
“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.
In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.

“If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”
He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.

Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living.
He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering bid to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.
“We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday.

“But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.”

blocks.caption: (From l to r) AfD party co-chair Tino Chrupalla, Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel a day after the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: The AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier.
after newsletter promotion

Merz, who has acknowledged that his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD.

He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority.
“And you won’t manage that in Germany either” at the federal level, Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.”

Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil.

He said that despite “clear evidence” a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airport last month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it.
Earlier from the podium, Weidel savoured her party’s resounding election victory, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership.

Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future.
Polls show Merz’s fractious coalition would not have a majority in a general election, which is not scheduled until 2029.
The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

articles.title: N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
articles.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency's says the facility is cause for "serious concern".

blocks.text: North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern".
The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium.
In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency said Pyongyang has also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site.

These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments.

"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week.
The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year.
In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility.
Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report.
Despite running one the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m.

"What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC.

"Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites."

The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said.
It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.

The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017.
The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017.

articles.title: Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
articles.summary: Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal…

image.caption: Protest about abducted Syrian women: Another example of the kinds of rumors circulating is that women from minority communities are being sold as sex slaves Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.

Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.

"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."
At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.
"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.

In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.
"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.
What is the 'house of sisters'?

Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.
There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority.

Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.

But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.
Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 ­­— have not been fully investigated.
A political football

Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.
Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.

"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.
"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."

So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently.

"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."
International influencers

A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."

In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.

blocks.caption: Christian neighborhood in Damascus: There have been reports of more attempts to convert others to Islam since the fall of the Assad regime, which treated proselytizing as a threat to national security Image: Mohammad Bashir Aldaher/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."

On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.

Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."
Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime.
The damage done?

"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.

"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."
Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.

Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.

blocks.caption: Syrians are still finding mass graves after 14 years of a civil war that has resulted in polarized opinions among localsImage: Ugur Yildirim/DIA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."
Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.

"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."
Stabilization first

"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.
In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.

blocks.caption: Every summer, Latakia's beaches in western Syria are a popular destination for thousands of Syrian holidaymakers Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.
For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.

"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."
Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.

articles.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
articles.summary: Germany's chancellor clashes with AfD leader Alice Weidel, saying her migration policy amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images/Reuters
Merz and Weidel faced off for the first time since Sunday's AfD election victory
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.
Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.
Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".
While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it make a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.
Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

blocks.caption: Map of eastern Germany highlighting the state of Saxony-Anhalt in white. Key locations marked include Magdeburg (the state capital), Querfurt and Leipzig within or near the highlighted area, and Berlin to the northeast. Poland is shown to the east and the Czech Republic to the south. An inset map…

blocks.text: As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.
Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.
The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

articles.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
articles.summary: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that…

image.caption: Bryson DeChambeau is owed an estimated $5.7m by LIV GolfImage: Jerod Ringwald/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: What has happened to LIV golf?
The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.
"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m), Jon Rahm ($7.5m) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7m).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model" but detail is thin and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.
What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding was so key to its business model that it gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.
Why is Saudi Arabia investing billions in sports?
Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia is scaling back many sporting plans, including for World Cup 2034Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city - 500-meter-high, built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.
What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

That too is unclear. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the The Players Championship or one of the four majors. DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
articles.summary: Heads of state from around the world came to Oslo to pay tribute to the late monarch.

image.caption: Harald reigned for 35 years, eschewing the modern tradition of abdicating in old ageImage: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral.
Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king.
Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service.
The procession and funeral will bring an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked and down-to-earth monarch at the age of 89.

blocks.caption: King Haakon (second from left) walked alongside his children and sisterImage: Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: Who is attending the funeral?

The funeral is being attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. This includes the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden.
Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are also attending.
Harald's son King Haakon VIII will be there alongside his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit.
Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship is also expected to be at the funeral.
Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest.

articles.title: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
articles.summary: President Abelardo de la Espriella has lifted a decade-long suspension on permits to carry legal firearms.

blocks.text: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public.

De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves".
The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation.
De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place.
While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word."

The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities.
But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro.
Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation.
De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun.
They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date.
Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals.
Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security.

De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year.
Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang.

articles.title: 'Hunted,' 'shattered,' 'scared': How victims say Canada's most prolific voyeur has altered their lives
articles.summary: CBC News has spent months going through court records and speaking with victims in the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada. Victims say it has left them feeling shattered, hunted and…

image.caption: 'It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault,' one woman tells others who are victims of a prolific voyeur. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: The 15-year-old wore her school uniform, unaware a stranger followed as she walked with her mother and brother through Victoria's Mayfair Shopping Centre.
A cellphone video would later show a voyeur trailing the family, before getting close enough to slip a camera beneath the girl's pleated skirt.
When police told the girl's mother, she faced a dilemma: tell her daughter, or keep it to herself?
"Learning my daughter's image had been taken and posted on child pornography websites was devastating," she wrote in a victim impact statement read in court earlier this year.
"I have carried significant stress over how I want to tell her and how she will cope with the information once she learns the truth."
The teen is one of 652 women and children filmed in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada.

Yin Yeung Derek Chan spent six years secretly recording victims throughout communities on southern Vancouver Island, filming through house windows and prowling malls and well-known stores in the heart of downtown Victoria.

In the year prior to Chan's 2024 arrest, the voyeur was creating more than a video a day, uploading footage and photos of victims to social media, porn sites and a personal website that had over a million views before it was taken down.
Chan was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison in May — but many of the photos and videos remain online. Only a fraction of the victims have been identified.

items: B.C. attorney general says potential victims of Saanich voyeur have 'right to know' key details from police

blocks.text: Despite wide reporting of the sentencing, many questions remain about the police investigation and the impact of Chan's crimes.
CBC News has spent months gathering court records, listening to audio of courtroom proceedings and reaching out to Chan's victims.
In her victim impact statement, one woman said watching the video Chan took of her "shattered" her sense of safety.
"Seeing myself through the eyes of someone who had been hiding, watching, deliberately capturing me without my knowledge or consent — it made me feel hunted," she said.
"This crime did not end when the recording stopped."
Chan used delivery job to access victims' homes

Chan came to Canada from Hong Kong as a child. Although Chan's lawyer said the 39-year-old identifies as gender fluid, police referred to Chan using male pronouns and some victims say they saw a man hovering nearby, phone in hand.
Crown prosecutor Paul Cheeseman said Chan worked as an Uber Eats delivery driver, using the job to access apartment building laundry rooms.
"[Police] found thousands of pairs of women's underwear in his house and a number of them were used," Cheeseman told the court.
"So it appears he was stealing women's underwear while he was doing these videos and deliveries."
Chan has a history of secretly recording women; in 2019, Chan was caught filming a woman in a changing room at a Forever 21.

During Chan's recent sentencing, the voyeur apologized to victims but offered little insight into a pattern of prolific offending. The judge said Chan compared it to the rush of "stealing a chocolate bar from a store" and attributed the crimes to "warm weather” in an earlier proceeding.
Saanich police have repeatedly declined to specify where Chan filmed victims, in spite of calls from B.C.'s attorney general to help potential victims know if they could be affected.

According to the court records, more than 400 victims were targeted at Value Village in Victoria, while about 80 were filmed at local Walmart locations. Others were recorded at Greater Victoria businesses, including Indigo Books, Munro's Books, Shoppers Drug Mart, Michaels, Mayfair Shopping Centre, Hillside Centre, and the Bay Centre mall.
A few were sunbathing at what is believed by police to be Willows Beach in Oak Bay.
Five people were recorded through the windows of their homes and apartments, at addresses in the James Bay, Fairfield, and Hillside neighbourhoods of Victoria.
Police also found about 100 hours of other videos Chan recorded of other women at gyms and malls that "don't rise to the level of criminal voyeurism," Cheeseman said.
'A part of my innocence was taken from me'
One victim told CBC News that Saanich police contacted her in January 2025 after an officer she knew recognized her in a video seized from Chan's home.
Until she saw the video, she didn’t know Chan had snuck up behind her in an Indigo Books to film up her dress — though she remembers seeing the voyeur.

"Him being so close to me was like the most icky feeling and thing to think about, like, how did I let someone get so close to me without noticing?" said the woman, whose identity is protected by a publication ban.
"It made me scared to think of, like someone could get that close to me without realizing, like what else could they have done to me?"
For a time after she found out, the woman says she was too afraid to go out alone in public, even to the grocery store.
Just weeks ago, a man in line at a dollar store started talking to her.
"I just like, shut down in my body," said the woman.
In victim impact statements, other women told the judge who sentenced Chan that they have difficulty holding down a job, struggle with mental health, and have changed the clothes they wear.

items: 1st known victim of Saanich voyeur calls for police, court reforms to prevent future offences

blocks.text: Some spend money on Ubers to avoid public transit. One victim said she got off a bus and walked almost an hour, because another passenger had a phone camera pointed her way.
The women said Chan's crimes have affected relationships, eroded their ability to trust others, and left them feeling powerless.
"I feel as though a part of my innocence was taken from me," wrote one victim, who was 17 and days out from her high school graduation when Chan filmed her.

Another victim was underage when Chan recorded her working as an employee at a mall. The incident triggered past trauma and she began to isolate herself. Her grades at a local college suffered, and she had to withdraw.
She said she was unable to maintain a job due to intense anxiety and fear in public spaces.
The woman said she gets counselling and financial support from WorkSafeBC, but the $4,900 she receives a year isn't enough to make ends meet.
"My life has been delayed and derailed, and my future seems uncertain," she said in her statement to the court.
"This offence did not just take away my sense of safety, it took away my independence, my ability to support myself, and my financial stability."
Some recordings still online
Cheeseman said Chan was well known in the online voyeurism community for posting videos, which were downloaded and reposted by other users.
"Mr. Chan has made it available for the entire world to revictimize these people," he said.
While police have gotten some recordings removed from Chan's personal website and Flickr, the prosecutor said officials have faced challenges in getting others taken down.

items: Girls in school uniforms among hundreds filmed by Saanich voyeur, court records reveal

blocks.text: A search of the username Chan used to upload many videos and images of the victims shows many are still easily found online on social media and porn websites.
One of these posts, on Reddit, is tagged "NSFW" — the site's label for explicit content.
Comments on this post, shown in court, ask Chan where to find the videos.
"We're all eager and ready to pay or something man you gotta bless us you got the finest bitches on camera," writes one user.
"Will u sponsor me?" Chan writes back to another, telling a third user the videos are "only open to payers."
Reddit did not respond to questions from CBC News about the post.

Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News, but Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that "the scale of this case was unprecedented and the impact on victims cannot be overstated."

"We recognize that once material has been distributed online it may not be possible to remove every copy, which remains an ongoing concern for many victims and represents an additional layer of victimization."
'None of it was your fault,' woman tells other victims
On May 21, the day of Chan's sentencing, Saanich police published a notice announcing the case publicly for the first time.

The victim who spoke to CBC News says it felt strange to see everyone discussing something she'd only told a few of those closest to her, especially as police promised to update her before the case became public — which she says they did not.
At first, she said it felt scary to read what people thought online about the case. But with time, it began to feel validating.

"It kind of made me feel like I was able to then be like, you know what, this was really messed up, and this happened to me, and I am allowed to feel violated by this situation, and I should allow myself time and space to have those feelings," the woman said.
"It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault."

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
articles.summary: Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post.
Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".
The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.

Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year.
"Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media.
"Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."

articles.summary:
President to give speeches on both days of unprecedented gathering

blocks.text: Republicans put Trump center stage for convention in US midterms gamble
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump is due to address Republicans tonight at the party’s first ever national convention ahead of the crucial midterm elections, with the GOP hoping to energize voters as it fights to hold its narrow congressional majorities.
The two-day gathering takes place in Dallas, marking a break from the longstanding tradition of holding national conventions only during presidential election years.
“It has never been done before, and will be a truly Historic Event,” Trump said in July while announcing the convention, promising the convention would feature “Great Entertainment”.
Trump first floated the idea for a convention last year, arguing that it would provide an opportunity to showcase his administration’s achievements since he returned to the White House in 2024.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.

Trump delivers this evening’s keynote speech and returns for Thursday’s finale after vice-president JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.
In other developments:

items: Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty. The US Supreme Court decided not to intervene to reinstate a Donald Trump-backed US House map, upholding a a ruling from the state’s highest state court that prevented the use of the map in the November elections. But shortly after a federal judge temporarily barred the state from using its old congressional maps in November.
The US military destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after a US navy warship was targeted with ballistic missiles. Iran had targeted the warship twice over two days, the US Central Command said.

The US will ban Canadian dairy products, motorcycles and most alcoholic beverages. The move marked an escalation in the ongoing trade war between the North American countries, and comes just after Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US goods.

Congressman Chris Pappas beat back progressive challenger Karishma Manzur in the New Hampshire Democratic primary for US Senate. Former senator John E Sununu, who is backed by Trump, won the state’s Republican Senate primary.

Lonnie G Bunch III announced he is stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution after seven years in the role amid Donald Trump’s unprecedented crackdown on the world’s largest museum’s autonomy.

The gifts were noted in the staffers’ annual financial disclosure forms that were published by the administration last week. Harp, Martin and Harris make $150,000 annually and Nauta is paid $175,000 a year, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress.

A White House official told the Associated Press that Trump “has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.”

The official did not say if any other staffers were given similar gifts from the president, but added that the cash gifts were not related to the “individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”

articles.title: South Korean students help plant narra seedlings on Mt. Malarayat
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — South Korean students joined a regreening activity that involved planting 100 narra tree seedlings at the foot of Mount Malarayat in Lipa City, Batangas, the Department of Environment…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — South Korean students joined a regreening activity that involved planting 100 narra tree seedlings at the foot of Mount Malarayat in Lipa City, Batangas, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said.

In a report on Tuesday, Sept. 8, the DENR office in Calabarzon said its Lipa community environment and natural resources office (Cenro) had partnered with ASEZ (Save the Earth from A to Z), a university student volunteer group of the World Mission Society Church of God, for the activity in Barangay Malitlit.
The agency said the initiative aimed to support the continuing rehabilitation and maintenance of the country’s forests.

“The program highlighted the important role of the youth in addressing environmental concerns, as well as the fact that environmental protection is a global responsibility that knows no nationality,” the DENR said.
Cenro Lipa also emphasized the importance of engaging young people in environmental protection efforts.
“It is important to raise their awareness and encourage their active participation in initiatives aimed at protecting the environment and natural resources,” the DENR said.

The narra, which is the Philippines’ national tree, is a large leguminous tree that can grow 30 to 40 meters tall. It produces fragrant yellow flowers that attract bees and typically blooms from February to May.
The species faces increasing threats from illegal logging, habitat loss, land conversion, and unsustainable harvesting. /mcm

articles.title: Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
articles.summary: The parents of Celeste Rivas Hernandez say execution "would be perfect" if D4vd is found guilty.

blocks.text: The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.
Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.
In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.
Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".
In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.
Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.
Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.
In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.
Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".
"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.
His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

articles.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or…

image.caption: Not even conspiracy theories help us come to terms with the unsettling events of September 11, 2001Image: Diane Bondareff/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.
That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.

If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job", orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.
Self-report data is an issue in conspiracy research
Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.
Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.
But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.

They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective, and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.

Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"

"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall.
Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.
In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-­being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.

This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.
Brain health: How to protect mental fitness and memory
Observing behavior can offer clues
There are ways of "triangulating" self-­report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional, or psychological, state.

For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability, or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.

But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).
"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.
The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'

Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.
There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.
Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the UK or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the US.
And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.
It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.
For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.
Watergate Anniversary
But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.

"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety, or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.

Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.

"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.
No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief
There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.

"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.
But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.
In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us, what psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.

But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety, and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.

articles.title: Policeman kills teacher wife at Thai school, kids safe: officials
articles.summary: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said. The gunman returned…

blocks.text: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said.
The gunman returned home after the shooting in Chonburi province, southeast of Bangkok, where police were negotiating his surrender.
The incident is the latest shooting to rock Thailand, a month after a teenager shot his grandparents and then five staff and a pupil at his school, before killing himself.
Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region, and past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.

Sayan Klomaon, chairman of Nong Pla Lai sub-district council, told AFP the gunman — a policeman local to the area — came to the school at about 10:30 am (0330 GMT) and talked with his wife before shooting her.
No students saw the incident, as it happened outside the classroom, he said, adding that the gunman then left to go home, and since then all the children had been picked up.
In a statement on Facebook, Chonburi Governor Naris Niramaiwong confirmed that all 44 children were safely evacuated along with three teachers and three other staff members.
He said police had surrounded the house where the gunman was and were negotiating his surrender.
The motive remains unclear.
Naris ordered the kindergarten closed and said psychological support will be provided to children and staff who witnessed the incident.
In 2022, an ex-policeman armed with a gun and a knife stormed a nursery in northern Thailand and killed 24 children and 12 adults, in one of the country’s deadliest massacres.

articles.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
articles.summary: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, in suitcases on planes or by exploiting legal loopholes to end up on dinnerplates. Where are the…

image.caption: Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque CountryImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels.

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.
"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

blocks.caption: Marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says only 12% of eels now survive the journey from the Sargasso SeaImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: so far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market.

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."
International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.
"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

blocks.caption: A small dam near Plentzia — obstacles like this can block eels on their migration routeImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eels smuggled in plain sight in regular suitcases along complex routes

Still, Stein, who did his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.
"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he said. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

blocks.caption: In Plentzia, where eel fishing has long been part of daily life, fishermen say the regional ban risks hurting those who follow the rules while illegal traders continue to profitImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: A species running out of time

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.
"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.
The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic.
